rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Viruses are the borderline of life: 20–300 nm particles of a single nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) wrapped in a capsid of capsomeres, sometimes within a host-derived envelope, with no metabolism, no ribosomes and no independent life — yet capable of replication, mutation and evolution inside a host. rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Virus = Nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) + Capsid (protein) [+ Envelope (lipid + glycoprotein)]
Lytic cycle: Adsorption → Penetration (injection) → Biosynthesis → Assembly → Release
Lysogenic cycle: Prophage integration → Replication with host → Induction → Lytic cycle

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Lytic vs lysogenic:** lytic kills the host immediately; lysogenic integrates as prophage and replicates with the host until induced to lyse.  ·  **Capsid vs envelope:** capsid = protein coat made of capsomeres; envelope = host-derived lipid membrane with spikes (present in influenza, HIV; absent in phage).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB expects a detailed T4 phage diagram and the 5-step lytic cycle.  ·  The "are viruses alive?" debate is a favourite exam discussion; present both arguments.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***T4 phage*** — complex head-tail virus of E. coli; the lytic-cycle textbook specimen.  ·  ***TMV*** — helical rod virus; first virus crystallised (Stanley, 1935).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: virus, structure, importance of virus, bacteriophage (within Introductory Microbiology).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Biology — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Label T4 phage  ·  Draw the lytic cycle (5 steps)

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "AP-B-M-L: Adsorb, Penetrate, Biosynthesise, Mature, Lyse."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Q.** What is a prophage? **Answer.** Phage DNA **integrated into the host bacterial chromosome** during the lysogenic cycle. It replicates passively with the host's DNA at every cell division and can later be induced (by stress) to excise and enter the lytic cycle.

rows.text: Most-tested: borderline-of-life reasoning (2024), T2 structure + reproduction (2022), lytic cycle (2024).  ·  Diagram-worthy: T2 phage labelled, lytic vs lysogenic cycles side by side.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Obligate parasitism:** a virus is a bundle of heredity without a metabolism — it borrows the host cell's ribosomes, enzymes and energy to copy itself.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Viruses: 20–300 nm, DNA or RNA (never both), nucleocapsid, no metabolism/ribosomes, replicate only in living host cells, crystallisable — borderline of life.  ·  T2 phage: head (dsDNA) + collar + contractile sheath + base plate + 6 tail fibres; host = E. coli.  ·  Lytic cycle: adsorption → penetration (DNA injection) → biosynthesis → maturation → lysis (lysozyme, 100–200 phages). Lysogenic: prophage integration.  ·  Importance: phage therapy, genetic-engineering vectors, Hershey–Chase DNA proof; but influenza, HIV, polio, TMV, foot-and-mouth.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Viruses are the most abundant biological entities on Earth — about 10^31 particles, ten times more than bacteria.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: ***HIV*** — enveloped RNA retrovirus using reverse transcriptase; causes AIDS.

rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Borderline of Life Viruses straddle the line between living and non-living: inside a host they replicate, evolve and respond; outside it they are inert crystals of protein and nucleic acid. rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Virion vs virus:** virion = the complete infectious particle outside a cell; "virus" is the broader term.  ·  DNA vs RNA viruses: know the key difference and one example of each.  ·  Mention the significance of the viral envelope (immune evasion, cell entry).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The 2024 lytic-cycle question was worth 4 marks — practise the five named steps in order with the diagram.  ·  "A virus is a piece of bad news wrapped in protein."  ·  Why can't viruses be cultured on artificial media like bacteria? **Answer.** Viruses have **no metabolism of their own** — no ribosomes, no ATP generation, almost no enzymes. They can only be assembled by hijacking a living host cell's machinery, so they replicate solely inside living cells.…
